stem: The chapter 'Through the Eyes of Travellers' reconstructs medieval Indian society mainly through the accounts of which three foreign travellers?
options: Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, and Francois Bernier
Megasthenes, Fa Xian, and Xuan Zang
Marco Polo, Vasco da Gama, and Columbus
Nicolo Conti, Domingo Paes, and Abdur Razzaq
solution: The chapter focuses on three major travellers whose writings are used to understand medieval India: Al-Biruni (an 11th-century scholar from Central Asia/Khwarizm), Ibn Battuta (a 14th-century Moroccan traveller), and Francois Bernier (a 17th-century French physician-traveller). Their accounts, written by 'outsiders', offer valuable perspectives on Indian society, though each must be read critically. So the three travellers are Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, and Bernier.

stem: Al-Biruni, who wrote a famous account of India, came from which region and reached India in association with whose campaigns?
options: Central Asia (Khwarizm); he came in the wake of Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions
France; as a physician to the Mughal court
solution: Al-Biruni (born 973 CE) came from Khwarizm in Central Asia (present-day Uzbekistan region). A great scholar, he was taken/came to the subcontinent in connection with the campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni (who raided India in the early 11th century) — Al-Biruni was among the scholars associated with Mahmud's court and travelled to the Punjab region, where he studied Indian learning. So he came from Central Asia in the wake of Mahmud of Ghazni's invasions.

stem: Al-Biruni's famous work on India, written in Arabic, is known as the __________.
solution: Al-Biruni's celebrated account of India is the Kitab-ul-Hind (also referred to by its Arabic title Tahqiq-i Hind), written in Arabic. It is a wide-ranging study of Indian religion, philosophy, sciences, customs, and social life, organised into many chapters. (The Rihla is Ibn Battuta's travelogue; 'Travels in the Mughal Empire' is Bernier's work; the Ain-i-Akbari is Abul Fazl's work.) So Al-Biruni's book is the Kitab-ul-Hind.

stem: To understand Indian traditions, Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and studied Indian texts. This shows that he:
options: Relied only on hearsay and rumour
Made a serious scholarly effort to understand Indian religion, philosophy, and sciences from original sources
Was hostile and refused to study Indian learning
Only described the food and clothing
solution: Al-Biruni made a serious scholarly effort to understand India: he learned Sanskrit, studied Indian religious, philosophical, and scientific texts (including works on astronomy, mathematics, and the Puranas), and tried to explain Indian ideas to a West/Central Asian audience, often comparing them with Greek, Islamic, and other traditions. He is admired for his relatively careful, systematic, and comparative approach (though he too faced barriers). So his learning of Sanskrit reflects a serious scholarly effort to understand India from its own sources.

stem: Al-Biruni identified several 'barriers' that, he felt, obstructed understanding between cultures. Which of the following did he mention as a barrier?
options: Language (the difficulty of Sanskrit); the difference in religious beliefs and practices; and the self-absorption/insularity of the Indians (their sense of superiority)
The distance of India from Central Asia only
The lack of any written texts in India
solution: Al-Biruni reflected on the difficulties/barriers to understanding between his own society and India. He mentioned barriers such as: language (Sanskrit was very different from Arabic/Persian and hard to master, and concepts did not translate easily); the difference in religious beliefs and practices; and what he saw as the self-absorption, insularity, and sense of superiority of the Indians (a reluctance to mix with or share knowledge with 'outsiders'). He tried to overcome these barriers through scholarship. So he named language, religious difference, and insularity as barriers.

stem: Al-Biruni described the Indian caste system and even compared it with the social divisions of other societies. He noted a system in Iran of four social categories, and he tried to understand the varna and jati order, but he was critical of the notion of __________.
options: Pollution/untouchability (the idea that certain things/persons become permanently impure)
solution: Al-Biruni described the caste system (the four varnas and the jatis) and compared Indian social divisions with those of other societies (e.g., the ancient Persian classes). While explaining the system, he was critical of the Brahmanical notion of pollution/impurity — the idea that certain occupations, things, or persons become permanently impure/polluted (as in untouchability). He argued (drawing partly on his own outlook) that according to nature everything that becomes impure can be purified/restored (e.g., the sun purifies, water cleanses), so the rigid Brahmanical concept of permanent pollution was, he felt, contrary to nature. So he was critical of the idea of pollution/untouchability.

stem: Ibn Battuta, the famous traveller who visited India in the 14th century, came from which city/country?
solution: Ibn Battuta (born 1304) was a traveller from Tangier in Morocco (North Africa). A well-educated man from a family of legal scholars, he set out on extensive travels across Africa, West Asia, India, China, and beyond over many years, and recorded his experiences. He reached India in the 14th century during the reign of the Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq. So Ibn Battuta came from Morocco.

stem: Ibn Battuta's book recording his travels is called the __________, and he preferred the knowledge gained from __________ over that from books.
solution: Ibn Battuta's travel account is called the Rihla (written in Arabic). Notably, Ibn Battuta valued the knowledge and insight gained from actual travel and personal experience of different lands and peoples more highly than knowledge gained merely from books/hearsay — he was an inveterate traveller who considered experiencing the world first-hand to be the best way to learn. So his book is the Rihla, and he prized personal travel/experience.

stem: During his stay in India, Ibn Battuta was appointed to an official post by the Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq. What position did he hold?
solution: The Delhi Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq, impressed by Ibn Battuta's learning, appointed him as the qazi (judge, administering Islamic law) of Delhi — a high and responsible office. Ibn Battuta held this position for some years before the Sultan later sent him as an envoy to China. His account thus reflects both an outsider's fresh perspective and an insider's experience of the Sultanate's administration. So he served as the qazi of Delhi.

stem: Ibn Battuta found many things in India remarkable and unfamiliar. He described the coconut and the __________ as strange/exotic fruits, showing how a traveller records the unfamiliar.
solution: As an outsider, Ibn Battuta was struck by many unfamiliar things in India and described them in detail for his readers. Among the novelties he described were the coconut (which he found remarkable, comparing it to a human head) and the paan (betel leaf, chewed for its stimulating and refreshing qualities). His careful description of such everyday items illustrates how a traveller notices and records what is unfamiliar to him but ordinary to locals. So he described the coconut and paan as exotic.

stem: Ibn Battuta was greatly impressed by the postal system of the Delhi Sultanate, which he found very efficient. This system included two kinds of postal service — one by horses and one by __________.
solution: Ibn Battuta was impressed by the efficient postal system (dak) of the Sultanate, which he described. There were two types: the horse-post (uluq), using relays of horses stationed at intervals; and the foot-post (dawa), using relays of foot-runners stationed at short intervals (every few miles), who could carry mail — and even goods — very rapidly across the country by running in relays. He noted it was even faster than the horse-post for news and could bring fruits and water quickly to the Sultan. So the two services used horses and foot-runners.

stem: Ibn Battuta noted that Indian agriculture was very productive, partly because the fertile soil allowed cultivators to grow how many crops a year in many regions?
options: Two crops a year (and sometimes more)
Only one crop every two years
solution: Ibn Battuta remarked on the fertility of the Indian soil and the productivity of agriculture, noting that in many regions farmers could raise two crops a year (a kharif and a rabi harvest) — and sometimes even more — because the soil was so fertile and easy to cultivate. This agricultural abundance supported a large population, extensive trade, and prosperous towns. So he observed that cultivators grew two crops a year.

stem: Ibn Battuta described Indian cities (like Delhi and Daulatabad) as densely populated and prosperous, with crowded bazaars. He portrayed towns as centres of __________.
options: Economic activity, crafts, and trade, with markets that were also hubs of social and cultural life
solution: Ibn Battuta described Indian cities as densely populated, prosperous, and full of opportunities. He portrayed towns and their bazaars/markets as bustling centres of economic activity — crafts, manufacturing, and trade — as well as hubs of social and cultural life (markets were not just places of buying and selling but also had spaces for social gatherings, performances, and religious activities, e.g., mosques and temples nearby). Cities like Delhi and Daulatabad were, he said, very large and cosmopolitan. So he saw towns as centres of economic and cultural activity.

stem: Ibn Battuta described the Indian practice of __________, which he found remarkable and disturbing — the custom of a widow burning herself on her husband's funeral pyre.
solution: Ibn Battuta described (among the customs he observed) the practice of sati — the burning of a widow on her deceased husband's funeral pyre. He found the practice remarkable and was disturbed by it, and he recorded an eyewitness-style account of a sati ceremony (noting that the ruler's permission was required). His account is one of the outsider descriptions of this custom. So the practice was sati.

stem: Francois Bernier, the third traveller, was a __________ from France who spent about twelve years in India, largely at the Mughal court.
solution: Francois Bernier was a French physician (doctor), as well as a political philosopher and historian. He came to India in the 17th century and stayed for about twelve years (c. 1656–1668), during much of which he was associated with the Mughal court — he was for a time attached to prince Dara Shukoh and later to a Mughal noble. His observations were shaped by his profession and his comparative (Europe-vs-India) outlook. So Bernier was a physician.

stem: Bernier's famous account of India is titled __________, and he constantly compared India with __________.
options: Travels in the Mughal Empire; Europe (especially France)
solution: Bernier's work is titled 'Travels in the Mughal Empire' (his account of India, dedicated to the French king Louis XIV). A distinctive feature of Bernier's writing is that he constantly compared what he saw in India (Mughal India) with conditions in Europe, and especially France — generally to show India in a negative/inferior light and Europe as superior. This comparative (and often prejudiced) framing shaped his account. So his book is 'Travels in the Mughal Empire', comparing India with Europe.

stem: One of the most influential (and much-debated) ideas Bernier put forward was that in Mughal India there was __________, which he argued had harmful consequences.
options: No private property in land — the king/state owned all the land ('crown ownership of land')
Widespread private ownership of land by peasants
solution: Bernier's most influential (and later much-criticised) idea was that in Mughal India there was NO private property in land — he claimed that the king/state (the Mughal emperor) was the owner of ALL the land ('crown ownership of land'), and merely assigned it to nobles. He argued that this supposed absence of private property in land had disastrous consequences: it discouraged investment and improvement, ruined agriculture, impoverished the peasantry, and led to a society of a rich, oppressive ruling class and a wretched, downtrodden mass, with no prosperous 'middle' class. So Bernier's claim was the absence of private property in land (crown ownership).

stem: Bernier's idea that Asian/Mughal rulers were despots who owned all land, leading to universal poverty, later fed into a European stereotype of the East known as __________.
solution: Bernier's picture of the Mughal (and Asian) ruler as an all-owning, arbitrary despot presiding over a land with no private property and hence universal poverty and stagnation, fed into a broader and very influential European stereotype known as 'Oriental Despotism' — the notion (developed by later Western thinkers, including Montesquieu and, in a related form, Marx's 'Asiatic mode of production') that Eastern societies were ruled by all-powerful despots owning all land, with stagnant economies and no checks on royal power. Modern historians reject this as an oversimplified and misleading stereotype (private property and rich mercantile classes did exist in Mughal India). So Bernier's idea contributed to the notion of Oriental Despotism.

stem: Modern historians argue that Bernier's claim that the Mughal state owned all land and that there was no private property was:
options: Completely accurate and confirmed by all evidence
Misleading/exaggerated — in reality there were rich merchant and landholding groups, artisans, and a flourishing trade, and land rights were more complex
Proof that India had no economy
solution: Modern historians regard Bernier's claim (no private property, all land owned by the king, universal poverty) as misleading and exaggerated, shaped by his European bias and comparative agenda. In reality, Mughal India had complex land-rights (peasants, zamindars with hereditary rights, etc.), flourishing internal and external trade, prosperous merchant and banking communities (like the sarrafs and the great merchants), rich artisans producing goods for export, and thriving towns — evidence of considerable commercial vitality and social differentiation, not the flat picture of a despot ruling over uniform misery. So Bernier's claim is now seen as misleading/exaggerated.

stem: Bernier's writings also described Indian society as sharply divided between a very rich ruling class and __________, painting a picture with no prosperous 'middle' state — a view historians now consider oversimplified.
options: An impoverished, downtrodden mass of people
solution: Bernier painted Indian (Mughal) society as sharply polarised — a small class of extremely rich and powerful rulers/nobles at the top, and a vast mass of impoverished, downtrodden people at the bottom — with (he claimed) no substantial prosperous 'middle' condition in between. Historians now consider this a distorted oversimplification: Mughal India in fact had a range of intermediate and prosperous groups — merchants, bankers, professionals, prosperous artisans and cultivators, service gentry, etc. So Bernier described a polarised society of rich rulers and an impoverished mass.

stem: Why must the accounts of travellers like Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, and Bernier be read CRITICALLY?
options: Because travellers always lie about everything

Because each traveller was an outsider whose observations were shaped by his own background, biases, purposes, and comparisons, so their accounts mix valuable information with misunderstanding and prejudice
Because their accounts are written in Indian languages
Because they never actually visited India
solution: Travellers' accounts must be read critically because each traveller was an OUTSIDER whose observations were shaped by his own cultural background, religious outlook, purposes, expectations, and points of comparison. Al-Biruni compared India with the Islamic and Greek worlds; Ibn Battuta noted whatever seemed strange and remarkable to a North African Muslim; Bernier constantly compared India (usually unfavourably) with Europe/France and had his own agenda. Their accounts therefore mix genuinely valuable eyewitness information (that Indian texts may not record) with misunderstandings, exaggerations, and prejudices. So we must weigh what they say critically, being aware of their biases. This is the central methodological lesson of the chapter.

stem: The value of travellers' accounts for historians lies especially in the fact that outsiders often:
options: Noticed and described everyday things and customs that insiders took for granted and did not bother to record
Copied Indian texts word for word
solution: A special value of travellers' accounts is that outsiders often noticed, found remarkable, and recorded everyday things, practices, and social customs that insiders (locals) took for granted and therefore rarely bothered to write down (e.g., the coconut and paan, the postal system, agricultural practices, food, markets, social customs). Because these ordinary details struck the foreigners as novel, they described them — giving historians information about daily life and society that Indian sources often omit. So outsiders' fresh eyes captured the everyday, which is precisely their value (used with due caution). This is a key point.

stem: Al-Biruni tried to make Sanskrit/Indian ideas understandable to his audience by comparing them with the ideas of which other traditions?
options: Greek, Islamic, and other (e.g., biblical/Sufi) traditions
solution: Al-Biruni adopted a comparative method: to explain unfamiliar Indian (Sanskritic) ideas to his readers, he compared and contrasted them with the ideas of other traditions he and his audience knew — especially the Greek (classical philosophical/scientific) tradition, and Islamic thought (as well as, at times, other religious traditions). This comparative approach was a notable feature of his scholarship and helped bridge cultures, even as he acknowledged the barriers to understanding. So he compared Indian ideas with Greek, Islamic, and other traditions.

stem: Ibn Battuta's travels were extraordinary in extent. Over roughly how long did his journeys across the world span, and how did he mostly travel?
options: Several decades, covering vast distances by land and sea (a lifetime of travel), mostly overland by caravan and by ship
Only along the Indian coast for a month
solution: Ibn Battuta was one of history's greatest travellers. His journeys spanned several decades (much of his adult life, from the 1320s onward), covering an enormous area — North and West Africa, West Asia, Central Asia, the subcontinent, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Southeast Asia, and China — mostly travelling overland by caravan (across deserts and mountains) and by ship across seas, facing many hardships and dangers. His long and wide-ranging travels give his Rihla great scope. So his travels spanned decades, mostly overland by caravan and by sea.

stem: In describing the position of slaves in the Delhi Sultanate, Ibn Battuta noted that slaves were:
options: Common — many were employed in domestic service, and some (especially those with skills or in the Sultan's service) could occupy varied positions; slaves were also bought and sold in markets
All set free by the Sultan
Only prisoners of war held briefly
solution: Ibn Battuta described the presence and roles of slaves in the Sultanate. Slaves were common; many were employed in domestic service (in households of the Sultan and nobles), some women slaves were employed as musicians, dancers, or for surveillance, and slaves were openly bought and sold in markets (and given as gifts). While many performed menial domestic labour, slaves' conditions and positions varied — some in royal or elite service could hold more privileged or specialised roles. His account is an important source on slavery in this period. So slaves were common and served in varied (mostly domestic) capacities and were traded in markets.

stem: The chapter uses these travellers' accounts to reconstruct which aspects of medieval Indian life?
options: A wide range — social customs, the caste system, the position of women and slaves, agriculture, cities and markets, trade, the postal and administrative systems, and everyday practices
solution: The chapter draws on the travellers' accounts to reconstruct a wide range of aspects of medieval Indian society: social organisation and customs (including the caste system, as seen by Al-Biruni), the position of women (e.g., sati) and slaves, the fertility and productivity of agriculture, the prosperity and life of cities and their bustling bazaars/markets, trade, the efficient postal and administrative systems (Ibn Battuta), and everyday items and practices — as well as broader questions like landholding and the nature of the state (Bernier). Thus the accounts illuminate social, economic, and cultural life, not just politics. So option 2 is correct.

stem: Which traveller's account most influenced later European thinking about the nature of Indian/Asian society and its economy?
options: Bernier's — his ideas (crown ownership of land, no private property, Oriental despotism) shaped later European debates
None had any influence in Europe
solution: Bernier's account was especially influential in shaping later European thinking about India and Asia. His ideas — that the Mughal/Asian state owned all the land (no private property), that this led to a despotic, stagnant, and impoverished society, and the resulting notion of 'Oriental Despotism' — were taken up and elaborated by later European philosophers and economists (e.g., Montesquieu, and echoes in Marx's concept of the 'Asiatic mode of production'). Thus Bernier's writings had a long and significant afterlife in Western thought (even though modern historians have discredited these ideas). So Bernier's account was the most influential in Europe.

stem: Al-Biruni is generally regarded by historians as a comparatively reliable and sympathetic observer because he:
options: Made a determined effort to learn the language, study original texts, and understand Indian ideas on their own terms, and tried to be objective (though not free of all bias)
Simply repeated Mahmud of Ghazni's propaganda
solution: Al-Biruni is generally regarded as a comparatively careful, serious, and relatively sympathetic (though not entirely bias-free) observer, because he made a determined effort to understand India properly: he learned Sanskrit, studied original Indian texts (in religion, philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, etc.), sought to grasp Indian ideas on their own terms, used a comparative method, and tried to describe things accurately and honestly (even acknowledging the 'barriers' to understanding). This scholarly rigour distinguishes his Kitab-ul-Hind. So he is valued for his serious, text-based, relatively objective effort. (He was not merely a mouthpiece for Mahmud's raids.)

stem: The three travellers came in different centuries. Arrange Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, and Bernier in the correct chronological order of their visits to India.
options: Al-Biruni (11th c.) → Ibn Battuta (14th c.) → Bernier (17th c.)
solution: The correct chronological order is: Al-Biruni came in the early 11th century CE (in the age of Mahmud of Ghazni); Ibn Battuta came in the 14th century CE (during the Delhi Sultanate, under Muhammad bin Tughlaq); and Francois Bernier came in the 17th century CE (during the Mughal period, in the time of Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb). So the order is Al-Biruni → Ibn Battuta → Bernier. Knowing this sequence (and the political context of each) is prelims-relevant.

stem: Match each traveller with the ruling power/period during which he visited India: Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta, and Bernier were respectively associated with the times of:
options: Mahmud of Ghazni (Ghaznavid); the Delhi Sultanate (Tughlaq); and the Mughals
The Mughals; the Guptas; the Cholas
The Cholas; the Mauryas; the Guptas
The Delhi Sultanate; the Mughals; the Ghaznavids
solution: The correct associations are: Al-Biruni — the era of Mahmud of Ghazni (the Ghaznavids), early 11th century; Ibn Battuta — the Delhi Sultanate under Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Tughlaq dynasty), 14th century; and Francois Bernier — the Mughal Empire (Shah Jahan/Aurangzeb), 17th century. Placing each traveller in his correct political context is important for understanding and dating his account. So the pairing in option 1 is correct.

stem: Ibn Battuta was struck by the cosmopolitan character of Indian cities, where he met people from many lands. This reflects that medieval Indian towns were:
options: Isolated and cut off from the world
Connected to wider networks of trade and travel, attracting merchants, scholars, and travellers from across Asia and Africa
solution: Ibn Battuta was impressed by the cosmopolitan character of Indian cities, where he encountered people, scholars, merchants, and travellers from many different lands (Central Asia, West Asia, Africa, etc.). This reflects that medieval Indian towns (like Delhi) were well connected to wider networks of trade, pilgrimage, and travel across Asia and Africa — hubs that attracted a diverse, mobile population. This contradicts any notion of India being isolated. So Indian towns were cosmopolitan and connected to wider networks.

stem: Assertion (A): Bernier's account of Mughal India presents a largely negative and impoverished picture. Reason (R): Bernier constantly compared India unfavourably with Europe (France) and argued that the absence of private property in land led to a despotic, stagnant, and poverty-stricken society. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Bernier's account paints a largely negative, impoverished picture of Mughal India. And the reason is (R) that Bernier constantly compared India unfavourably with Europe (particularly France), and built his account around the thesis that the (supposed) absence of private property in land and the despotic, all-owning nature of the Mughal state led to economic stagnation, ruin of agriculture, and widespread poverty. This comparative-and-despotism framework directly produces the negative picture (A). So R correctly explains A. (Modern historians reject the accuracy of this picture.)

stem: Assertion (A): Al-Biruni criticised the Brahmanical idea that pollution, once incurred, is permanent. Reason (R): He argued, partly from the observation of nature, that whatever becomes impure can subsequently be purified/restored. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that Al-Biruni was critical of the Brahmanical concept of pollution/impurity (as in untouchability), especially the idea that impurity, once incurred, was permanent. And the reason is (R) that he argued — drawing partly on the observation of nature — that everything that falls into a state of impurity can, by natural processes, be purified and restored to its original condition (the sun, air, and water cleanse and purify; nature strives to restore purity). Since impurity is not permanent in nature, he found the rigid Brahmanical notion of permanent pollution unreasonable and contrary to nature. So R correctly explains A.

stem: Which of the following is an accurate general statement about how the three travellers differed?
options: Al-Biruni was a scholar who studied Indian texts deeply; Ibn Battuta was an experiential traveller who prized first-hand observation of the novel and strange; and Bernier was a physician-philosopher who wrote comparatively and analytically (often to India's disadvantage)
None of them wrote anything down
solution: The three travellers differed markedly in background and approach: Al-Biruni (11th c., Central Asia) was primarily a SCHOLAR who deeply studied Sanskrit texts and Indian sciences, using a careful comparative method; Ibn Battuta (14th c., Morocco) was an EXPERIENTIAL traveller who valued first-hand observation, delighting in describing the novel, strange, and everyday things he encountered; and Bernier (17th c., France) was a PHYSICIAN and political philosopher who wrote analytically and comparatively, systematically comparing India with Europe (usually to India's disadvantage). Recognising these different perspectives helps in reading each account critically. So option 2 correctly captures the differences.

stem: The Rihla of Ibn Battuta and the Kitab-ul-Hind of Al-Biruni were both originally written in which language?
solution: Both Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind and Ibn Battuta's Rihla were originally written in Arabic (the scholarly and literary language of the wider Islamic world to which both authors belonged). (Bernier's 'Travels', by contrast, was written in French.) Knowing the language of the original sources is relevant to understanding how they reached and influenced different audiences. So both Al-Biruni's and Ibn Battuta's works were in Arabic.

stem: Ibn Battuta's willingness to travel to distant and unfamiliar lands, even at great personal risk, reflects a broader medieval reality of:
options: Extensive connections and mobility across the medieval world — of travellers, pilgrims, scholars, merchants, and envoys moving between Africa, Asia, and beyond
The absence of any trade routes
solution: Ibn Battuta's decades-long journeys across Africa, Asia, and beyond — and the fact that he could find employment, hospitality, and fellow travellers along the way — reflect a broader medieval reality of extensive connections and mobility across the 'Afro-Eurasian' world: networks of trade routes (overland caravan routes and maritime routes), pilgrimage, scholarship, and diplomacy along which people, goods, and ideas moved between distant regions. Medieval societies were far from isolated. So his travels reflect wide-ranging medieval connectivity and mobility. This is an important broader point.

stem: Bernier dedicated his account of India and addressed his writings to audiences in Europe. His main purpose in comparing India with Europe was often to:
options: Praise India as superior in every way
Present India (and 'the East') as inferior/despotic and, by contrast, portray Europe as superior and better-governed
Encourage Europeans to adopt Indian customs
Simply record neutral facts with no agenda
solution: Bernier wrote for a European audience (dedicating his work to the French king and engaging European intellectuals), and his comparative method typically served to present India and 'the East' as inferior, despotic, and backward, while portraying Europe (especially France) as superior and better-governed. This comparative-and-hierarchical framing (the East as the despotic 'other' against which Europe's virtues were highlighted) reveals his agenda and bias, which is why his account must be read critically. So his purpose in comparing was largely to show India as inferior and Europe as superior.

stem: Which statement about the caste system does Al-Biruni's account help historians with, despite its limitations?
options: It provides an outsider's contemporary description and analysis of the varna/jati order (and Al-Biruni's own critical reflections on it), which can be compared with Brahmanical texts
It shows caste was invented in the 19th century
It is a complete and unbiased record
solution: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind provides historians with a valuable outsider's contemporary (11th-century) description and analysis of the Indian caste system — the four varnas and the jatis — along with his own critical reflections (e.g., on pollution). Although his account has limitations (he relied heavily on Brahmanical/Sanskrit texts and normative sources, so it may reflect the ideal more than lived reality, and carries his own perspective), it is still useful because it can be compared and cross-checked with Brahmanical texts and other evidence, offering an external viewpoint on the social order. So it gives an outsider's description and analysis of caste, useful with caution. This nuanced use of the source is the point.

stem: A key methodological caution the chapter raises about Al-Biruni's description of Indian society is that it may reflect __________ rather than actual social practice.
options: The normative/ideal picture drawn from Brahmanical (Sanskrit) texts
The economic statistics of the empire
solution: A key methodological caution is that Al-Biruni depended largely on Sanskrit (Brahmanical) texts and Brahmana informants for his understanding of Indian society (especially the caste system). As a result, his description may reflect the NORMATIVE/IDEAL picture set out in those prescriptive Brahmanical texts (how society was supposed to be ordered) rather than the actual, lived social practice (which, as we know from other evidence, was often more fluid and varied). Historians therefore treat his account of caste as partly reflecting the Brahmanical ideal. So the caution is that it may reflect the normative/ideal (textual) picture rather than actual practice.

stem: The efficient dak (postal) and administrative arrangements described by Ibn Battuta indicate that the Delhi Sultanate had:
options: A fairly well-organised state apparatus capable of rapid communication and control over a large territory
solution: Ibn Battuta's admiring description of the efficient postal system (both horse-post and foot-runner relays) — which sped news, orders, and even goods across the realm faster than ordinary travel — indicates that the Delhi Sultanate possessed a fairly well-organised and sophisticated state apparatus, capable of rapid communication, coordination, and control over a large territory. Such an effective communication network is a mark of a functioning centralised administration. So it indicates a well-organised state apparatus. This is a useful inference from the traveller's account.

stem: Considering all three, the chapter's broader lesson about foreign accounts is that they are:
options: Indispensable but partial sources — rich in unique, everyday detail, yet shaped by the traveller's own perspective and therefore to be corroborated and interpreted with care
More reliable than any Indian source
Identical to one another in content
solution: The chapter's broader lesson is that foreign travellers' accounts are indispensable but partial sources for Indian history: they are rich in unique observations — especially of everyday life, customs, economy, and administration — that Indian sources often omit; yet they are inevitably shaped by each traveller's own cultural background, purposes, and biases. Therefore historians must value them for their distinctive information while reading them critically — corroborating their claims with other evidence and interpreting them with awareness of the author's perspective. So they are indispensable but partial, to be used with care. This balanced conclusion is the heart of the chapter.

stem: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind is organised into __________ chapters, covering topics from religion and philosophy to astronomy, customs, weights and measures, and laws.
solution: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind is a large and systematically organised work, divided into around 80 chapters (approximately eighty), covering a very wide range of subjects — religion and philosophy, festivals, astronomy and astrology, the sciences (including mathematics), literature, customs and practices, social life, weights and measures, iconography, laws, and metrology, among others. This comprehensive, topic-wise organisation reflects his scholarly, encyclopaedic approach. So the Kitab-ul-Hind has about 80 chapters.

stem: Ibn Battuta eventually left India when the Sultan sent him on a mission. Where was he sent as an envoy?
options: To China (as an ambassador of Muhammad bin Tughlaq)
solution: After serving as qazi of Delhi, Ibn Battuta was sent by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq as his envoy/ambassador to China. His journey to China (via the Maldives, Sri Lanka, Bengal, and Southeast Asia) was eventful and full of hardships (including shipwreck and robbery). This mission and the further travels it entailed added greatly to the range of his Rihla. So he was sent as an envoy to China.

stem: Which of the following best explains why Indian society's own records often did NOT describe the everyday matters that fascinated the travellers?
options: Everyday things were so familiar/ordinary to insiders that they were taken for granted and seemed not worth recording, whereas to outsiders they seemed novel and noteworthy
The travellers forbade Indians from writing
There were no everyday activities in India
solution: Indian society's own records (texts, chronicles) often did not describe everyday matters (like common foods, the coconut and paan, ordinary customs, market life) simply because these things were so familiar and ordinary to insiders that they were taken for granted — not considered remarkable or worth writing down. To outsiders/travellers, however, these same things appeared novel, strange, and noteworthy, so they described them in detail. This is exactly why travellers' accounts are so valuable for filling gaps in our knowledge of daily life. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The chapter cautions that even the seemingly 'factual' descriptions in travel accounts should be checked because a traveller might:
options: Misunderstand what he saw, rely on hearsay for some things, generalise from limited experience, or be influenced by his own expectations and prejudices
solution: The chapter cautions that even apparently 'factual' descriptions in travel accounts must be checked, because a traveller might misunderstand what he saw (unfamiliar customs can be misread), rely on hearsay or second-hand information for some things he did not witness directly, over-generalise from limited or localised experience to the whole country, or be influenced by his own expectations, cultural assumptions, and prejudices. All of these can distort even sincere reporting. Hence the need to corroborate and interpret critically. So option 2 lists the reasons for caution.

stem: Ibn Battuta noted that in some regions and communities of India, women enjoyed relatively greater freedom or unusual customs. His observations remind historians that:
options: Social customs (including those concerning women) varied considerably across regions and communities in India
Women had no role in society
All of India followed identical rules
solution: Ibn Battuta, travelling across many regions of India (and neighbouring areas like the Maldives), noticed considerable variation in social customs from place to place — including customs concerning women, marriage, and social life (for instance, he found practices in some coastal/island societies quite different from those elsewhere). His observations remind historians that India was not socially uniform: customs, including the position and treatment of women, varied significantly across different regions and communities. So option 2 is correct — Indian social customs were diverse, not uniform.

stem: Bernier's detailed descriptions of Mughal cities, the imperial camp, and artisans are valuable because, despite his biases, he provides:
options: Rich, first-hand observations of urban life, crafts, and the workings of the Mughal court and economy that historians can use (critically) alongside other sources
solution: Despite his prejudices and his 'oriental despotism' thesis, Bernier provides rich, detailed first-hand observations of many aspects of 17th-century Mughal India — the great cities (like Delhi and Agra), the vast imperial camp when the emperor travelled, the working conditions and skills of artisans, markets, and the functioning of the court and economy. Historians can use these detailed descriptions (critically, filtering out his biases) as valuable evidence, corroborated with other sources. So his account, though biased, offers usable first-hand observations of urban and economic life.

stem: The word 'Rihla', the title of Ibn Battuta's book, essentially means a __________.
solution: 'Rihla' is an Arabic term meaning a journey or travels — and, as a literary genre, a 'travelogue' or account of one's travels. Ibn Battuta's Rihla is thus, quite literally, his 'book of travels', recording the many lands, peoples, and experiences he encountered on his decades-long journeys. So 'Rihla' means a travelogue/account of travels.

stem: Taken together, why does the chapter choose travellers from three DIFFERENT centuries and backgrounds rather than one?
options: Because comparing accounts from different periods and perspectives (11th, 14th, and 17th centuries; scholar, experiential traveller, and comparative philosopher) gives a richer, multi-angled, and more critical understanding of change and continuity in medieval Indian society
Because only three accounts survive in the world
Because they all wrote in the same year
solution: The chapter deliberately chooses three travellers from different centuries (11th, 14th, 17th) and very different backgrounds and approaches (Al-Biruni the Central Asian scholar; Ibn Battuta the Moroccan experiential traveller; Bernier the French physician-philosopher) so that, by comparing their accounts, students gain a richer, multi-angled view of medieval Indian society across time — noting both continuities and changes — and learn to weigh different perspectives and biases against one another. This comparative, multi-perspective approach yields a more critical and nuanced understanding than any single account could. So option 2 is correct.

stem: The three foreign travellers whose accounts form the basis of the chapter 'Through the Eyes of Travellers' are:
options: Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta and Francois Bernier
Marco Polo, Vasco da Gama and Columbus
solution: The chapter reconstructs medieval Indian society through the accounts of Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta and Francois Bernier.

stem: Al-Biruni came from __________ (Uzbekistan region) and reached India in association with the campaigns of Sultan Mahmud of Ghazni.
solution: Al-Biruni came from Khwarizm in Central Asia and came to India in association with the campaigns of Mahmud of Ghazni.

stem: Al-Biruni's famous work on India, written in Arabic, is known as the:
solution: Al-Biruni's account of India is the Kitab-ul-Hind, written in Arabic.

stem: The Kitab-ul-Hind is organised into about __________ chapters covering religion, philosophy, astronomy, customs, laws, etc.
solution: The Kitab-ul-Hind is organised into about 80 chapters covering a wide range of subjects.

stem: Al-Biruni learned __________ to study Indian texts and understand Indian traditions.
solution: Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit to study Indian texts directly and understand Indian traditions.

stem: Al-Biruni tried to make Indian ideas understandable by comparing them with the ideas of which other traditions?
solution: Al-Biruni compared Indian ideas with Greek, Islamic and other traditions to make them intelligible to his audience.

stem: Al-Biruni was critical of the Brahmanical notion that pollution, once incurred, is:
solution: Al-Biruni criticised the Brahmanical idea that pollution, once incurred, is permanent, arguing that what becomes impure can be purified again.

stem: Ibn Battuta, who visited India in the 14th century, came from:
solution: Ibn Battuta came from Tangier in Morocco.

stem: Ibn Battuta's book recording his travels is called the:
solution: Ibn Battuta's travel account is called the Rihla.

stem: The word 'Rihla' essentially means a:
solution: 'Rihla' means a travel account or record of a journey.

stem: Ibn Battuta preferred the knowledge gained from __________ over that gained from books.
solution: Ibn Battuta valued knowledge gained through travel and personal experience over that from books.

stem: During his stay in India, Ibn Battuta was appointed by Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq to the post of:
solution: Ibn Battuta was appointed the qazi (judge) of Delhi by Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

stem: Ibn Battuta was eventually sent by the Sultan as an envoy to:
solution: Ibn Battuta was sent by Muhammad bin Tughlaq as an envoy to China.

stem: Ibn Battuta was greatly impressed by the Delhi Sultanate's efficient postal system, which used horses and __________.
solution: The postal system had a horse-post and a foot-runner (dak) service, which Ibn Battuta found remarkably efficient.

stem: Ibn Battuta described the __________ and the coconut as strange/exotic fruits.
solution: Ibn Battuta described the paan (betel leaf) and the coconut as strange and exotic to him, illustrating how travellers record the unfamiliar.

stem: Ibn Battuta described the Indian practice of __________, a widow burning herself on her husband's funeral pyre, which he found remarkable and disturbing.
solution: Ibn Battuta described the practice of sati, which he found remarkable and disturbing.

stem: Ibn Battuta's travels across the world spanned several decades, and he mostly travelled by:
solution: Ibn Battuta's journeys spanned decades, travelling largely overland by caravan (with some sea voyages), across Asia, Africa and India.

stem: Francois Bernier was a __________ from France who spent about twelve years in India, largely at the Mughal court.
solution: Francois Bernier was a French physician (doctor) who spent about twelve years in India, mostly at the Mughal court.

stem: Bernier's famous account of India is titled 'Travels in the Mughal Empire', and he constantly compared India with:
solution: Bernier's 'Travels in the Mughal Empire' constantly compared India with Europe, especially France.

stem: One of Bernier's most influential (and debated) claims was that in Mughal India there was:
options: no private property in land (the state owned all land)
solution: Bernier argued that in Mughal India there was no private property in land — the state (king) owned all land — a claim historians now dispute.

stem: Bernier's idea that Asian rulers were despots who owned all land, leading to poverty, fed into a European stereotype known as:
solution: Bernier's ideas fed into the European stereotype of 'Oriental Despotism' — the notion of tyrannical Asian rulers and stagnant societies.

stem: Modern historians argue that Bernier's claim that the Mughal state owned all land was:
options: largely inaccurate/exaggerated (there was private property and a prosperous economy)
solution: Historians argue Bernier's claim was largely inaccurate; there was private landholding and a substantial, prosperous economy in Mughal India.

stem: Bernier portrayed Indian society as sharply divided between a very rich ruling class and __________, with no prosperous middle — a view now considered oversimplified.
solution: Bernier described society as divided between the very rich and the impoverished masses, with no prosperous middle — an oversimplified view.

stem: The Kitab-ul-Hind and the Rihla were originally written in which language?
solution: Both Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind and Ibn Battuta's Rihla were originally written in Arabic.

stem: Ibn Battuta noted that Indian agriculture was very productive, allowing cultivators in many regions to grow __________ crops a year.
solution: Ibn Battuta noted the fertile soil allowed cultivators to grow two crops a year in many regions, indicating high productivity.

stem: Ibn Battuta described Indian cities like Delhi and Daulatabad as:
options: densely populated, prosperous centres with crowded, vibrant bazaars
solution: Ibn Battuta described Indian cities as densely populated, prosperous centres of economic and cultural activity with crowded bazaars.

stem: Ibn Battuta was struck by the cosmopolitan character of Indian cities, meaning they were:
options: home to people from many different lands and cultures
solution: Indian cities were cosmopolitan, home to people from many lands — reflecting their role as centres of trade and culture.

stem: In the correct chronological order of their visits to India, the three travellers are:
options: Al-Biruni (11th c.), Ibn Battuta (14th c.), Bernier (17th c.)
solution: In order: Al-Biruni (11th century), Ibn Battuta (14th century) and Bernier (17th century).

stem: The three travellers were respectively associated with the times of:
options: Mahmud of Ghazni/Ghaznavids, the Delhi Sultanate (Tughlaqs), and the Mughals
solution: Al-Biruni came with the Ghaznavids, Ibn Battuta during the Delhi Sultanate (Tughlaqs), and Bernier during the Mughals.

stem: Why must travellers' accounts be read CRITICALLY?
options: travellers viewed India through their own cultural lens, could misunderstand things, and had their own purposes and biases
solution: Travellers saw India through their own cultural assumptions, sometimes misunderstood what they saw, and had their own purposes and biases, so their accounts must be read critically.

stem: The value of travellers' accounts for historians is that outsiders often:
options: noticed and recorded everyday things that locals took for granted and did not write down
solution: Outsiders often noticed and recorded ordinary, everyday details that locals took for granted and did not record — valuable to historians.

stem: Indian society's own records often did NOT describe the everyday matters that fascinated the travellers because:
options: such ordinary things were taken for granted and not thought worth recording by locals
solution: Locals took everyday matters for granted and rarely thought them worth recording, so travellers' notice of them is especially valuable.

stem: Al-Biruni is regarded as a comparatively reliable and sympathetic observer because he:
options: made a genuine effort to learn Sanskrit and understand Indian texts and traditions on their own terms
solution: Al-Biruni is respected because he learned Sanskrit and made a serious, sympathetic effort to understand Indian texts and traditions on their own terms.

stem: A methodological caution about Al-Biruni's description of Indian society is that it may reflect __________ rather than actual social practice.
options: the Brahmanical (textual/normative) view rather than the real practice
solution: Al-Biruni relied heavily on Brahmanical (normative) texts, so his description may reflect the ideal/textual view rather than actual social practice.

stem: Bernier's detailed descriptions of Mughal cities, the imperial camp and artisans are valuable because, despite his biases, he provides:
options: rich, first-hand observations of Mughal urban life, crafts and administration
solution: Despite his biases, Bernier provides rich first-hand observations of Mughal cities, the imperial camp, crafts and administration, valuable to historians.

stem: The chapter chooses travellers from three DIFFERENT centuries and backgrounds rather than one because:
options: together they give a fuller, multi-perspective picture of medieval India across time and viewpoints
solution: Using travellers from different centuries and backgrounds gives a fuller, multi-perspective picture of medieval India across time and viewpoints.

stem: Ibn Battuta noted that in some regions and communities of India, women enjoyed relatively greater freedom or unusual customs, reminding historians that:
options: Indian society was diverse, with varied practices across regions and communities
solution: Such observations remind historians that Indian society was diverse, with practices (including women's status) varying across regions and communities.

stem: Bernier's main purpose in comparing India with Europe was often to:
options: highlight what he saw as India's inferiority/differences and instruct/warn European audiences
solution: Bernier compared India with Europe largely to highlight what he saw as its differences/inferiority and to inform (and sometimes warn) European audiences.

stem: Which of the following accurately states how the three travellers differed?
options: they came from different regions, centuries and backgrounds, and had different purposes and perspectives
they all came in the same year
solution: The three differed in their regions of origin, centuries, backgrounds, purposes and perspectives, giving varied windows onto medieval India.

stem: Which traveller's account most influenced later European thinking about Indian/Asian society and economy?
solution: Bernier's account most influenced later European thinking (e.g., the idea of 'Oriental Despotism') about Indian/Asian society and economy.

stem: The chapter cautions that even seemingly 'factual' descriptions in travel accounts should be checked because a traveller might:
options: exaggerate, misunderstand, rely on hearsay, or be influenced by bias
solution: Travellers might exaggerate, misunderstand, rely on hearsay or be influenced by their biases, so even factual-seeming descriptions must be checked.

stem: Al-Biruni identified 'barriers' obstructing understanding between cultures, such as language, religious/cultural differences, and:
options: the self-absorption/insularity and conceit of communities
solution: Al-Biruni cited barriers such as language, religious and cultural differences, and the insularity/conceit that made communities dismissive of others.

stem: Assertion (A): Bernier's account of Mughal India presents a largely negative and impoverished picture. Reason (R): He constantly compared India unfavourably with Europe and argued that the absence of private land property led to a despotic, stagnant, poverty-stricken society. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: Bernier's unfavourable comparison with Europe and his 'no private property' thesis produced a largely negative, impoverished picture.

stem: Assertion (A): Al-Biruni criticised the Brahmanical idea that pollution, once incurred, is permanent. Reason (R): He argued, partly from observing nature, that whatever becomes impure can subsequently be purified. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true and R correctly explains A
A is true but R is false
solution: Both are true and R explains A: reasoning from nature that the impure can be purified, Al-Biruni criticised the notion of permanent pollution.

stem: Taken together, the chapter's broader lesson about foreign accounts is that they are:
options: valuable but must be read critically, weighing the traveller's perspective, purpose and biases
solution: Foreign accounts are valuable sources but must be read critically, taking account of each traveller's perspective, purpose and biases.

stem: Which of the following BEST captures the central message of the chapter 'Through the Eyes of Travellers'?
options: The accounts of Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta and Bernier offer valuable outsider perspectives on medieval Indian society, but must be read critically, mindful of each traveller's viewpoint, purpose and biases
solution: The chapter concludes that the accounts of Al-Biruni, Ibn Battuta and Bernier are valuable outsider windows onto medieval Indian society, but must be read critically with awareness of each traveller's perspective, purpose and biases.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Through the Eyes of Travellers' is that:
options: Foreign travellers' accounts are worthless for Indian history

The writings of visitors like Al-Biruni (11th c.), Ibn Battuta (14th c.), and Bernier (17th c.) are valuable windows onto medieval Indian society — its social structure (caste, the position of women and slaves), its agriculture, cities, markets, trade, and administration — precisely because outsiders noticed and recorded everyday things insiders ignored; yet since each account was shaped by the traveller's own background, purposes, and biases (from Al-Biruni's textual scholarship to Bernier's Europe-centred idea of oriental despotism), these sources must always be read critically, corroborated, and interpreted with care
Medieval India had no contact with the outside world
All three travellers wrote exactly the same things
solution: The chapter's overall message is that foreign travellers' accounts are precious but partial sources for reconstructing medieval Indian history. The writings of Al-Biruni (Kitab-ul-Hind, 11th century, in the age of Mahmud of Ghazni), Ibn Battuta (Rihla, 14th century, under Muhammad bin Tughlaq of the Delhi Sultanate), and Francois Bernier ('Travels in the Mughal Empire', 17th century, Mughal era) open windows onto Indian society — its social structure and caste, the position of women (sati) and slaves, the fertility of agriculture, the prosperity of cities and bazaars, trade, and administration (like the efficient postal system) — often capturing everyday details that Indian sources took for granted and left unrecorded. At the same time, each account was shaped by its author's distinct background, purposes, and biases: Al-Biruni the careful scholar dependent on Brahmanical texts; Ibn Battuta the experiential traveller delighting in the novel; Bernier the comparative, Europe-centred writer who propounded the misleading idea of Mughal 'crown ownership of land' and 'oriental despotism'. Therefore these sources, while indispensable, must always be read critically — with awareness of the traveller's perspective — and corroborated with other evidence. This balanced use of travellers' accounts is the central lesson — option 2.
